procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a lower court within the jurisdiction of the Allahabad High Court, as the case involves a conviction under s. 302 (likely murder) which would originate in a trial court.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 8, 1968, of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 2305 of 1965.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Allahabad High Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 2305 of 1965, and rendered a judgment and order on February 8, 1968. The outcome of the appeal in the High Court is not explicitly stated, but since the appellant is challenging his conviction, it can be inferred that the High Court upheld the conviction.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached by the appellant, Matru @ Girish Chandra, who challenged his conviction under s. 302. The Supreme Court granted special leave to appeal, indicating that they found sufficient grounds to review the High Court's decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether the evidence regarding the identification of the articles was reliable enough to sustain a conviction.

facts: The articles were allegedly recovered from the appellant on June 1, 1964.
The identification test for these articles was conducted on October 23, 1964, nearly four months after the recovery.
The reason given for the delay was the need to procure similar articles to mix with the recovered ones.
The Court found the witnesses to the recovery itself were not implicitly reliable and required corroboration from a "more disinterested and dependable source."
A key item, a ring, was noted to be of a "common design and easily available."
law: Identification tests do not constitute substantive evidence.
The primary purpose of identification tests is to help the investigating agency confirm they are proceeding on the right lines.
Evidence regarding the recovery of articles from an accused's possession is not acceptable without proper corroboration from a disinterested and dependable source.
application: The Court was first unimpressed by the evidence of the articles' recovery, deeming it uncorroborated and unreliable. It stated that if the recovery evidence is weak, the identification test is of "little help to the prosecution."
The Court found the nearly four-month delay in conducting the identification test to be a major flaw.
The Court explicitly described the manner in which the delayed identification was held as "highly unsatisfactory."
The fact that the ring was of a common design further weakened the reliability of its identification.
Based on these weaknesses, the Court concluded that it was not possible to hold beyond a reasonable doubt that the recovered articles were the same ones missing from the deceased's house.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the evidence regarding the identification of the articles as unreliable. The Court found that the initial recovery of the items was not supported by dependable evidence, and the identification test itself was fatally flawed by a long and unsatisfactory delay, the common nature of the items, and the overall uninspiring nature of the prosecution's evidence on this point.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution had established beyond a reasonable doubt that the articles in question were recovered from the appellant's possession.

facts: The prosecution's case relied on evidence that a spectacle case, spectacles, and a gold ring were recovered from the appellant, Matru, upon his arrest.
A recovery memo, Ex. Ka-1, documented this recovery.
The trial court and High Court had previously relied on this recovery as a key incriminating circumstance.

However, the Supreme Court noted several issues with this evidence: the spectacles and case were not mentioned in the initial First Information Report (F.I.R.), and the ring was described as being of a "common design and easily available."
law: For evidence of recovery to be accepted, it must be supported by proper corroboration from a disinterested and dependable source.

In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the evidence must be scrutinized to determine if the chain of circumstances is so complete that it leads only to the conclusion of the appellant's guilt, excluding any reasonable possibility of innocence.
application: The Court found the testimony of the witnesses to the recovery to be "far from impressive" and the story of the recovery "difficult to accept on its face value."
It noted that one witness gave no details about the articles or the search of the appellant.
The Court determined that the evidence regarding the recovery was not acceptable because it lacked corroboration from a "more disinterested and dependable source."
The weak identification of the items—the common design of the ring and the omission of the other items from the F.I.R.—further undermined the prosecution's claim.
The Court concluded that it was not safe to hold that the articles were actually recovered from the appellant's possession as alleged.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the prosecution's argument, finding that the evidence regarding the recovery of the articles from the appellant's possession was unreliable, uncorroborated, and not sufficient to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The Court found it unsafe to rely on the testimony of the witnesses and noted weaknesses in the identification of the recovered items.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the evidence regarding the identification of the articles was reliable enough to sustain a conviction.
appellant_arguments: The police investigation and the identification of the articles were unreliable.
A witness stated in cross-examination that they would not be able to recognize the recovered articles.
A witness could not recall key details, such as when the articles were shown to the contractor or who made the entry in the record.
There was a noted discrepancy that the spectacle case was old while other mixed cases were new.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution's case was established by the evidence relating to the recovery of articles belonging to the deceased.
The testimony of prosecution witnesses (P.W. 2 and P.W. 10) and the recovery memo (Ex. Ka-1) proved the identity of the articles.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution had established beyond a reasonable doubt that the articles in question were recovered from the appellant's possession.
appellant_arguments: The circumstantial evidence, including the alleged recovery, was not sufficient to establish the appellant's complicity in the crime.
The police investigation, which included the recovery, was assailed as being unreliable.
respondent_arguments: An officer testified that he searched the appellant's person in the presence of witnesses and recovered a case containing spectacles and a ring from the right 'phant' of his 'dhoti'.
A recovery memo (Ex. Ka-1) was prepared and sealed on the spot, and signatures/thumb impressions of witnesses were obtained.
A witness corroborated the officer's testimony, stating that the articles were recovered from the appellant's person and a memo was prepared on the spot.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: While Article 136 of the Constitution does not confer a right of appeal, it grants the Supreme Court discretionary power to scrutinize and appraise evidence in criminal appeals under special circumstances to ensure that injustice has not occurred.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the evidence presented by the prosecution was insufficient to sustain a conviction, as it amounted only to suspicion rather than proof beyond a reasonable doubt. The court concluded it was not safe to hold that the articles in question were recovered from the appellant, the identification of those articles was unsatisfactory, and the alleged motive was not of a strong and impelling nature.
legal_tests_applied: In a case of circumstantial evidence, the evidence must not exclude the reasonable possibility of the appellant's innocence.
Suspicion however strong cannot take the place of proof.

Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court has discretionary power to scrutinize and go into the evidence in special circumstances in order to satisfy itself that injustice has not been done. Special circumstances include cases of circumstantial evidence where the identification of articles is unsatisfactory.
reasons_appellant_arguments_succeeded: The court found the identification of the stolen articles to be unsatisfactory, noting a specific discrepancy: 'The case of the spectacle is old one whereas the mixed cases were new'.

The court concluded that it was not safe to rely on the evidence to establish that the articles were recovered from the appellant's possession, stating, 'do not find it safe on this evidence to hold that the articles men• tioned in Ex. Ka-1 were recovered from the appellan• s puss.:s-B'.
The court determined that the motive evidence, based on a letter of questionable admissibility, was not of a 'strong and impelling nature so as to induce the murder of Omwati and her infant child.'
The court held that the totality of the prosecution's evidence 'may at best give rise only to a suspicion against the appellant; but suspicion however strong cannot take the place of proof.'
reasons_respondent_arguments_failed: The respondent's reliance on the testimony of P.W. 2 and P.W. 10 was deemed insufficient, as the court found this evidence, even when coupled with the motive, only gave rise to suspicion.
The respondent's evidence regarding the recovery of articles, including the recovery memo (Ex. Ka-1), was rejected by the court as not being safe to rely upon for a conviction.
policy_considerations: The Court exercised its discretionary power under Art. 136 to intervene and appraise the evidence for itself because the case had exceptional features (circumstantial evidence, unsatisfactory identification, acquittal of co-accused) and it needed 'to satisfy itself that irijustice has not been done.'
